Sticker attacks have been shown to be effective against object detectors, such as YOLO and Faster R-CNN [You Cannot Easily Catch Me: A Low-Detectable Adversarial Patch for Object Detectors]. These attacks can be used to hide objects from detection or to cause misclassification. For example, a sticker can be designed to make a stop sign appear as a speed limit sign to a detector [Adversarial Patch Camouflage against Aerial Detection]. Sticker attacks can also be used to attack person detectors, such as those used in surveillance systems [Fooling Automated Surveillance Cameras: Adversarial Patches to Attack Person Detection].

Another type of physical-world adversarial attack is camouflage attacks, where a camouflage texture is applied to an object or worn by a person to evade detection [Physically Realizable Natural-Looking Clothing Textures Evade Person Detectors via 3D Modeling]. records.section: Defense Mechanisms Against Visual Adversarial Attacks
records.content:
Adversarial Training and Input Preprocessing are two prominent defense mechanisms against visual adversarial attacks. Adversarial Training involves training a model on a dataset that includes adversarial examples, which are inputs designed to mislead the model. This approach has been shown to improve the robustness of models against adversarial attacks [Fighting Gradients with Gradients: Dynamic Defenses against Adversarial Attacks]. On the other hand, Input Preprocessing defenses transform or purify inputs before they are fed into the model, aiming to remove or reduce the effects of adversarial perturbations [Test-time Adversarial Defense with Opposite Adversarial Path and High Attack Time Cost].

Adversarial Training has been widely adopted as a defense mechanism against adversarial attacks. The basic idea is to train a model on a dataset that includes both clean and adversarial examples. This approach has been shown to improve the robustness of models against adversarial attacks [Adversarial Training Versus Weight Decay]. However, Adversarial Training has some limitations. For example, it can be computationally expensive and may not provide robustness against all types of attacks [Efficient Adversarial Training With Transferable Adversarial Examples]. Additionally, Adversarial Training may not transfer well from digital perturbations to physical-world attacks [Defending Against Transfer Attacks From Public Models].

Input Preprocessing defenses, on the other hand, aim to transform or purify inputs before they are fed into the model. These defenses can be used to remove or reduce the effects of adversarial perturbations [PuriDefense: Randomized Local Implicit Adversarial Purification for Defending Black-box Query-based Attacks]. For example, image preprocessing techniques such as image compression, filtering, or transformation can be used to defend against adversarial attacks [Improving FDI Detection for PMU State Estimation Using Adversarial Interventions and Deep Auto-Encoder]. Additionally, input normalization and randomization can also be used to defend against adversarial attacks [Robustness to Adversarial Attacks in Learning-Enabled Controllers].

One of the key challenges in defending against visual adversarial attacks is the transferability of attacks from digital perturbations to physical-world attacks. While Adversarial Training and Input Preprocessing defenses can provide robustness against digital perturbations, they may not transfer well to physical-world attacks [Characterizing Attacks on Deep Reinforcement Learning]. This is because physical-world attacks can be more complex and nuanced than digital perturbations, and may require more sophisticated defense mechanisms [Module-wise Adaptive Adversarial Training for End-to-end Autonomous Driving].

Recently, there has been a growing interest in developing defense mechanisms that can provide robustness against both digital and physical-world attacks. For example, [Game Theoretic Mixed Experts for Combinational Adversarial Machine Learning] proposes a game-theoretic framework for ensemble adversarial attacks and defenses. This framework can be used to develop defense mechanisms that can provide robustness against both digital and physical-world attacks. Additionally, [A Closer Look at the Adversarial Robustness of Information Bottleneck Models] proposes a novel approach to defending against adversarial attacks using information bottleneck models.

In conclusion, Adversarial Training and Input Preprocessing are two prominent defense mechanisms against visual adversarial attacks. While Adversarial Training can provide robustness against digital perturbations, it may not transfer well to physical-world attacks. Input Preprocessing defenses, on the other hand, can be used to remove or reduce the effects of adversarial perturbations, but may not provide robustness against all types of attacks. Developing defense mechanisms that can provide robustness against both digital and physical-world attacks is an active area of research, and recent approaches such as game-theoretic frameworks and information bottleneck models show promise in addressing this challenge [The Power of Many: Synergistic Unification of Diverse Augmentations for Efficient Adversarial Robustness]. 

Furthermore, [Enhancing Adversarial Robustness via Test-time Transformation Ensembling] shows that ensembling different transformations can improve the robustness of models against adversarial attacks. This approach can be used in conjunction with Adversarial Training and Input Preprocessing defenses to provide additional robustness against adversarial attacks. Additionally, [DARD: Dice Adversarial Robustness Distillation against Adversarial Attacks] proposes a novel approach to defending against adversarial attacks using distillation-based methods.

In terms of future research directions, there are several areas that need to be explored. For example, developing defense mechanisms that can provide robustness against both digital and physical-world attacks is an active area of research. Additionally, exploring the use of novel architectures and training methods, such as graph neural networks and meta-learning, may provide additional robustness against adversarial attacks [Teach Me to Trick: Exploring Adversarial Transferability via Knowledge Distillation]. Furthermore, developing more sophisticated evaluation metrics and benchmarking protocols is necessary to accurately assess the robustness of models against adversarial attacks [Evaluation Metrics and Benchmarking]. 

Overall, defending against visual adversarial attacks is a complex and challenging task that requires a comprehensive approach. By combining Adversarial Training, Input Preprocessing defenses, and novel architectures and training methods, we can develop more robust models that can withstand both digital and physical-world attacks. Additionally, ongoing research in this area is exploring new and innovative approaches to defending against adversarial attacks, such as [Boosting Adversarial Transferability using Dynamic Cues] and [On the Limitations of Stochastic Pre-processing Defenses]. These approaches show promise in addressing the challenges of defending against visual adversarial attacks and provide a foundation for future research in this area.

Adversarial Training and Input Preprocessing

The vulnerability of deep learning models to adversarial attacks has sparked a surge of research into defense mechanisms. Two prominent approaches to defending against visual adversarial attacks are adversarial training and input preprocessing. Adversarial training involves training a model on a dataset that includes adversarial examples, with the goal of increasing the model's robustness to such attacks. Input preprocessing, on the other hand, involves transforming or purifying the input data before it is fed into the model, in order to remove or mitigate the effects of adversarial perturbations.

Adversarial training has been shown to be an effective method for improving model robustness [Fighting Gradients with Gradients: Dynamic Defenses against Adversarial Attacks]. By training a model on a dataset that includes adversarial examples, the model can learn to recognize and resist such attacks. However, adversarial training can be computationally expensive and may require large amounts of training data. Additionally, adversarial training may not always transfer well to physical-world attacks, where the adversarial perturbations may be different from those seen in the digital domain [Defending Against Transfer Attacks From Public Models].

Input preprocessing, on the other hand, involves transforming or purifying the input data before it is fed into the model. This can be done using a variety of techniques, such as image denoising or compression [PuriDefense: Randomized Local Implicit Adversarial Purification for Defending Black-box Query-based Attacks]. Input preprocessing can be an effective method for defending against adversarial attacks, as it can remove or mitigate the effects of adversarial perturbations. However, input preprocessing may not always be effective against strong attacks, and may require careful tuning of parameters to achieve optimal results [On the Limitations of Stochastic Pre-processing Defenses].

One of the key challenges in defending against visual adversarial attacks is the transferability of attacks from the digital domain to the physical world. Adversarial attacks that are effective in the digital domain may not always be effective in the physical world, and vice versa [Characterizing Attacks on Deep Reinforcement Learning]. This is because the physical world introduces a range of complexities and nuances that are not present in the digital domain, such as lighting, shading, and texture. As a result, defense mechanisms that are effective in the digital domain may not always transfer well to the physical world.

Despite these challenges, there have been a number of successful defenses against visual adversarial attacks in the physical world. For example, [Module-wise Adaptive Adversarial Training for End-to-end Autonomous Driving] proposes a module-wise adaptive adversarial training method for end-to-end autonomous driving models. This method involves training a model on a dataset that includes adversarial examples, and adapting the model's parameters to improve its robustness to such attacks. The results show that this method can significantly improve the robustness of autonomous driving models to adversarial attacks in the physical world.

Another example is [SHIELD: Defending Textual Neural Networks against Multiple Black-Box Adversarial Attacks with Stochastic Multi-Expert Patcher], which proposes a stochastic multi-expert patcher method for defending against black-box adversarial attacks. This method involves training a model on a dataset that includes adversarial examples, and using a stochastic patcher to transform the input data before it is fed into the model. The results show that this method can significantly improve the robustness of textual neural networks to black-box adversarial attacks.

In addition to these examples, there have been a number of other successful defenses against visual adversarial attacks in the physical world. For example, [Adversarial Training on Purification (AToP): Advancing Both Robustness and Generalization] proposes an adversarial training on purification method for defending against adversarial attacks. This method involves training a model on a dataset that includes adversarial examples, and using a purification method to transform the input data before it is fed into the model. The results show that this method can significantly improve the robustness and generalization of models to adversarial attacks.

Overall, defending against visual adversarial attacks in the physical world is a complex and challenging task. However, by using a combination of adversarial training and input preprocessing, it is possible to significantly improve the robustness of models to such attacks. Further research is needed to develop more effective defense mechanisms, and to better understand the challenges and limitations of defending against visual adversarial attacks in the physical world [Game Theoretic Mixed Experts for Combinational Adversarial Machine Learning].

Metrics for Evaluating Adversarial Attacks

Evaluating the effectiveness of physical adversarial attacks is crucial to understanding their potential impact on real-world systems. Various metrics have been proposed to assess the success of these attacks, including attack success rate, robustness, transferability, and stealthiness. In this subsection, we will summarize the key metrics used to evaluate physical adversarial attacks and the benchmarks and protocols used to report them.

Attack success rate is a fundamental metric used to evaluate the effectiveness of adversarial attacks [Adversarial catoptric light: An effective, stealthy and robust physical-world attack to DNNs]. It measures the percentage of successful attacks out of the total number of attempts. A higher attack success rate indicates a more effective attack. For example, [Adversarial catoptric light: An effective, stealthy and robust physical-world attack to DNNs] reported an attack success rate of 83.5% in simulated environments.

Robustness is another critical metric used to evaluate physical adversarial attacks [Patch Attack Invariance: How Sensitive are Patch Attacks to 3D Pose?]. It measures the ability of an attack to withstand various environmental factors, such as distances, angles, and lighting conditions. A robust attack can maintain its effectiveness even when the environmental conditions change. For instance, [Adversarial Infrared Geometry: Using Geometry to Perform Adversarial Attack against Infrared Pedestrian Detectors] demonstrated that their attack can achieve a high success rate even at different distances and angles.

Transferability is a metric used to evaluate the ability of an attack to generalize across different models and scenarios [Revisiting Transferable Adversarial Images: Systemization, Evaluation, and New Insights]. A high transferability indicates that an attack can be effective against multiple models and scenarios, making it more threatening. For example, [Benchmarking Adversarial Patch Against Aerial Detection] reported that their attack can achieve a high success rate against different models and scenarios.

Stealthiness is a metric used to evaluate the ability of an attack to remain undetected [Hide and Seek: on the Stealthiness of Attacks against Deep Learning Systems]. A stealthy attack can evade detection by human observers or other detection mechanisms. For instance, [RFLA: A Stealthy Reflected Light Adversarial Attack in the Physical World] proposed a stealthy attack that can remain undetected even in the physical world.

In addition to these metrics, various benchmarks and protocols have been proposed to report the results of physical adversarial attacks. For example, [PADetBench: Towards Benchmarking Physical Attacks against Object Detection] proposed a benchmark for evaluating physical attacks against object detection models. The benchmark includes various metrics, such as attack success rate, robustness, and transferability, to provide a comprehensive evaluation of physical adversarial attacks.

[Selective Adversarial Attacks on LLM Benchmarks] also proposed a protocol for evaluating the selectivity of adversarial attacks on large language models (LLMs). The protocol includes metrics such as attack success rate, transferability, and stealthiness to evaluate the effectiveness of selective adversarial attacks.

Furthermore, [How Stealthy is Stealthy? Studying the Efficacy of Black-Box Adversarial Attacks in the Real World] proposed a framework for evaluating the stealthiness of black-box adversarial attacks. The framework includes metrics such as attack success rate, transferability, and stealthiness to evaluate the effectiveness of black-box adversarial attacks.

In conclusion, evaluating physical adversarial attacks requires a comprehensive set of metrics, including attack success rate, robustness, transferability, and stealthiness. Various benchmarks and protocols have been proposed to report the results of physical adversarial attacks, providing a comprehensive evaluation of their effectiveness. By using these metrics and benchmarks, researchers can develop more effective defense mechanisms against physical adversarial attacks and improve the security of real-world systems.
